messages.author: b5a3634251802902
messages.subject: Effects of minprob on mqmscan
parts:
Hi Karl,


I have a population of 93 RILs genotyped at 637 markers and I'd like to map QTLs that explain observed variation in a trait. The following is what I have been doing:


qtl.cross = read.cross(“mm”, file=”rils.cross.txt”, mapfile=”rils.map.txt”, crosstype=”riself”)

qtl.cross = subset(qtl.cross, ind=ntyped(qtl.cross)>=550)             


As you can see, I removed individuals with less than 550 markers genotyped, and this yields the remaining data with about no more than 15% missing genotypes. I attached a summary plot for my data named: “rils.cross.summary.png”.


I follow a may-be rule of thumb to choose minprob = 0.15 as suggested in MQM-tour.pdf (setting minprob to the percentage of missing data).


aug.cross.15 = mqmaugment(qtl.cross, minprob=0.15, verbose=T)


And because the map consists of many markers at the same positions, I used jittermap to add a little bit space in between. I then pick up cofactors and run mqmscan.


aug.cross.15 = jittermap(aug.cross.15, amount=0.1)

setcofactors = mqmsetcofactors(aug. cross.15, 10)

mqm_backw.15 = mqmscan(aug. cross.15, setcofactors, cofactor.significance=0.02, verbose=T)


I plot the mqmscan results as attached “mqm.backw.minprob15.png”.


Then I tried to play around with mqmaugment a bit by choosing different values to minprob, and re-run mqmscan with new augmented data.


aug.cross.25 = mqmaugment(qtl.cross, minprob=0.25, verbose=T)

aug.cross.30 = mqmaugment(qtl.cross, minprob=0.3, verbose=T)


However, when I compare the results of these mqmscan results, I found there are some differences. Some peaks show up in one but not in others, and some small peaks become larger in others.


So my first question is about the first phenomenon I saw. Which one of mqmscan results I should follow upon, and how can I choose minprob value in mqmaugment? 


And I tried to figure out the latter phenomenon by looking at the number of augmented individuals. It turns out aug.cross.15, aug.cross.25, and aug.cross.30 have 304, 375, and 370 individuals after augmentation. And if I understand correctly, the more augmented genotypes give more confidence (bigger peaks). But I should expect aug.cross.15 to have more augmented individuals than the other two, am I correct here? I reasoned this means there are individuals failed to be augmented. But I did not see warnings or messages talking about this. Could you please tell me how can I get such info?


My first question is about the first phenomenon I saw ("Some peaks show up in one but not in others"). Which one of mqmscan results I should follow upon, and how can I choose minprob value in mqmaugment? 


I apologize for this long long description of my problems. I'd appreciate any help!


cheers,

Simo

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Effects of minprob on mqmscan
parts:
Personally, I'd prefer to first look at the results of interval mapping from scanone(), either with method="em" or method="hk".

I'm not a strong proponent for MQM. Others may comment in support.

But your genotypes, for the RILs you retained, are quite complete. Rather than use augmentation, you might simply impute the missing genotypes, using the fill.geno() function, and then apply mqmscan.

The LOD curves here look a bit strange, with the many large and precise peaks. Do the peaks all correspond to cofactors?

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Effects of minprob on mqmscan
parts:
Hi Karl,

Thanks very much for helping here.

I did run scanone function with standard interval mapping and HK regression (for these, I did not run fill.geno before running scanone). There are peaks consistent with what I got from mqmscan but with much much less LOD. Running 1000 permutations with HK regression gives a LOD of 2.66 at 5%. This leaves only the highest peak on chr1. 

With only fill.geno function, mqmscan gives many more and even higher peaks. They are very suspicious especially ones on chr1, where high peaks are followed by immediate drop-downs. I guess those came from the warnings in thhe verbose output which showed many negative LODs.

 And you were right about most of the peaks corresponding to cofactors. Does this mean those peaks are likely artificial and the high LOD is inflated by cofactors?

I also did run stepwiseqtl which the best model (pLOD=0.8) consists only one QTL on chr1, consistent with results of scanone but not ones of mqmscan. Does this mean the actual model is a single-QTL? 

I went ahead using makeqtl and fitqtl using this single-QTL model. The following is the summary:

Method: Haley-Knott regression
Model:  normal phenotype
Number of observations : 82

Full model result
----------------------------------
Model formula: y ~ Q1

df       SS         MS      LOD     %var Pvalue(Chi2)    Pvalue(F)
Model  1 13.89703 13.8970290 3.278337 16.81586 0.0001021091 0.0001302116
Error 80 68.74538  0.8593173
Total 81 82.64241

Estimated effects:
-----------------
est       SE      t
Intercept  0.03427  0.10249  0.334
1...@15.5    -0.41421  0.10300 -4.021

The pve is about 17% and I expect more than one QTL contributing to this trait. Do you recommend I try to addqtl or addpairs using this main effect QTL as basic model? 

Thanks for your suggestions so far.
Simo

parts:
I said "With interaction, some loci on chr2 and chr5 got a bit bumped up compared to additive model." It should be chr2 and chr4 instead.

Method: Haley-Knott regression

Number of observations : 82

----------------------------------

df       SS        MS      LOD     %var Pvalue(Chi2)    Pvalue(F)

On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 11:38:56 AM UTC-5, Simo wrote:
Hi Karl,

I controlled for the major locus on chr1 and performed a scan for additional loci with and without allowing interaction. With interaction, some loci on chr2 and chr5 got a bit bumped up compared to additive model. But still none of them is beyond the permutation threshold of 2.66, and so then I am indeed looking at a single-QTL, right? The attached are the LOD curves. Thanks!

Simo

On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 11:03:45 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
If you control for the main locus on chromosome 1 and perform a scan for additional loci, are there any significant peaks? As stepwiseqtl() is indicating just the one locus, I'd guess not.

I'd be inclined to trust the results with the single major locus.

karl
